pages.name: A warm-up
pages.task: Seawater runs at 2 m/s through a pipe of 20 cm². How many litres pass each second?
pages.why: Flow is area × speed. 20 cm² is 0.002 m². So 0.002 × 2 = 0.004 m³ pass each second. A cubic metre is 1000 litres, so that is 4 L/s.

pages.name: What goes in comes out
pages.text: You just found the [[flow]] in this pipe, 4 L/s. Water barely squeezes, so the flow is the same at every section. Flow is area × the water's average speed. A throat of 5 cm² is a quarter of the pipe's area. So the same 4 L/s must move four times as fast there, at 8 m/s. That is [[continuity]]. In the throat the dots stretch apart.

pages.name: Before the columns
pages.task: Three thin columns will stand on this pipe. One is before the throat, one is on it and one is after it. The water speeds up from 2 to 8 m/s in the throat. How will the throat's column stand?
pages.why: Speeding up needs a push. Going into the throat, the pressure behind each bit of water must beat the pressure in front. So the pressure is lowest where the water is fastest. After the throat the water slows, and its pressure comes back.

pages.name: The columns
pages.text: Speeding up needs a push. Here only the pressure can give it. Going into the throat, the arrow behind the slug beats the one in front. So the pressure falls as the speed rises. Each column stands as high as its pressure holds it, so the throat's stands lower. After the throat the water slows, and its column stands back up. A real venturi gets most of the drop back, not all.

pages.name: Into a narrower pipe
pages.task: Water flows at 1.5 m/s in a pipe of 12 cm². It enters a section of 4 cm². How fast does it go there?
pages.why: The same flow passes both sections, so area × speed is the same. 12 × 1.5 must equal 4 × v. So v = 1.5 × 12 ÷ 4 = 4.5 m/s. A third of the area means three times the speed.

pages.name: Where the energy goes
pages.text: Pressure is itself energy in each cubic metre. Pushing 1 m³ of water in against 1 Pa takes 1 J. Moving water also carries [[½ρv²]] of kinetic energy in each cubic metre. With no friction, the two add to the same total along a level pipe. That is [[Bernoulli's principle]]. Before the throat, 150 + 2.1 makes about 152 kPa. In the throat, about 119.2 + 32.8 makes the same.

pages.name: How much lower?
pages.task: Seawater flows at 1 m/s in a pipe of 15 cm², into a throat of 5 cm². How much does the pressure change?
pages.why: The throat is a third of the area, so the water goes three times as fast, at 3 m/s. The drop is ½ρ times the change in the speed squared. That is ½ × 1025 × (3² − 1²) pascals, about 4.1 kPa. The pressure falls, because the water speeds up.

pages.name: A flow meter
pages.text: The drop grows with the speed squared. The speed is in step with the flow. So twice the flow gives four times the drop. At 2 L/s the drop is about 7.7 kPa, a quarter of 30.8. pages.name: Read the flow
pages.task: The flow is hidden, and the throat is 5 cm². The columns differ by about 7.7 kPa. What is the flow?
pages.why: At 4 L/s this throat drops 30.8 kPa. 7.7 kPa is a quarter of that. The drop goes with the flow squared, so a quarter of the drop means half the flow. That is 2 L/s. An [[orifice plate]], a flat plate with a hole in it, measures flow the same way. A sharp-edged one comes with a correction factor, its [[discharge coefficient]]. A [[Pitot tube]] is another meter. It measures the water's speed.

pages.name: Smooth or eddying
pages.text: Flow can glide in smooth layers or churn in eddies. Which you get depends on the speed, the bore and how thick the liquid is. Engineers roll these into one figure, the [[Reynolds number]]. Below about 2000, flow is smooth. Above about 4000, it usually eddies. Neither edge is fixed. Some put the upper one as high as 10 000. In between, a flow can go either way. Faster, wider and thinner flows are more likely to eddy.
pages.alt: The pipe with thin seawater moving fast, drawn as churning, wavy lines and swirls: it eddies. Below, a Reynolds number scale: smooth below about 2000, eddies above about 4000 or higher, and either way between.

pages.name: Which runs smooth?
pages.task: Which flow is most likely to run in smooth layers?
pages.answer: Thick, cold oil creeping through a small pipe
pages.why: Smooth layers need a low Reynolds number. That means slow flow, a small bore and a thick liquid. The thick, cold oil has all three. Seawater at 2 m/s is thinner and faster, so it is more likely to eddy. A wider pipe makes eddies more likely still.

pages.name: Flow to drop
pages.task: Seawater flows at 3 L/s through a pipe of 15 cm², into a throat of 6 cm². How big is the drop from pipe to throat?
pages.why: First the speeds. 3 L/s is 0.003 m³/s. In the pipe, 0.003 ÷ 0.0015 = 2 m/s. In the throat, 0.003 ÷ 0.0006 = 5 m/s. The drop is ½ × 1025 × (5² − 2²) pascals, about 10.8 kPa.

pages.name: Back to metres
pages.task: The drop to a throat is 30.8 kPa, in seawater. How much lower does the throat's column stand?
pages.why: A column h tall stands on a pressure of ρgh. So h is the drop ÷ ρg. That is 30,800 Pa ÷ (1025 × 9.81), about 3.1 m. In seawater, each 10 kPa is about 1 m of column.
